item.title: Parents Are AI-Generating Pictures of Their Kids Instead of Paying for School Photos
item.description:
"ChatGPT for the win."

The post Parents Are AI-Generating Pictures of Their Kids Instead of Paying for School Photos appeared first on Futurism.
item.content:encoded:
Why shell out for the mundane headshots by a school photographer when you could supercharge your kids’ portrait with the power of AI?

That’s a calculation more and more parents are making these days, choosing to tap into generative AI tools like ChatGPT to fast-track school picture day. According to Fast Company, parents are taking to social media to brag up how much AI saved them on their children’s’ school print package — usually in the range of $25 to $60 per.

One TikTok from influencer Carlie Bond showed off the hack: first, parents take some phone pictures of their children standing in front of a plain-colored wall, before tossing them into ChatGPT with the prompt “keep them exactly the same but make it look like a school picture.”

ChatGPT then adds a milquetoast background, reminiscent of school photos taken by typical bulk-photo companies like Lifetouch.

“We took our own and let my good friend Chat help us out,” Bond bragged, “and honestly… I’m not mad about how they turned out.”

“ChatGPT for the win,” one TikTok user replied.

Other parents observed by FastCo used AI to “remove” watermarks from scans of sample school photos, which they’d otherwise have to pay to clean up.

Of course, both use cases involve feeding a likeness of your child to a corporate AI model, where the images which will surely be used to train the next iteration of AI tools. Simply put, once a parent uploads those images, they’ll never get them back. Given the ethical and privacy risks involved, parents trying to save a buck on school photos might be wise to just take the pictures themselves, and leave ChatGPT behind.

item.title: Anthropic Reports User to the Police
item.description:
Watch what you tell Claude.

The post Anthropic Reports User to the Police appeared first on Futurism.
item.content:encoded:
With mounting pressure on AI labs to curb the many real-world harms their products cause consumers, it’s never been clearer that they’re monitoring users’ conversations.

Just ask Carli Michelle Heller, a woman arrested in Bonita Springs, Florida after allegedly telling Anthropic’s chatbot Claude about her plan to “shoot up” a nearby sheriff’s office.

According to WINK News, Heller was charged with making a written threat of violence — a second-degree felony in Florida — after Anthropic’s internal monitoring software flagged her chat logs for human review. After being viewed by a human employee at Anthropic, WINK reports, the company determined that Heller’s plans rose to the level of a credible threat, ultimately informing local police.

As Lee County Sheriff Carmine Marceno told local reporters in a statement, the woman admitted to using Claude like a “diary,” apparently unaware that her chat history could be read by Anthropic employees.

There’s a genuine tension between user privacy and the responsibility of AI companies to try to head off violent events. In the aftermath of the February mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, Canada, for instance, it quickly emerged that the perpetrator had relied heavily on ChatGPT to plan her shooting.

Not only had OpenAI staffers known about those chat logs prior to the shooting — they had been flagged for human review months prior — but company executives even tried to hide and later downplay their product’s role in encouraging the deadly attack.

While Anthropic’s own track record on real-world harm is wretched, it seems the company is at least trying to avoid the same kind of incident — though with near-endless chatbot options now on the market, it could already be too late to prevent the next AI-assisted tragedy.

item.title: Meta Insiders Convinced Muse Is Going to End Up Leaking the Bank Accounts and Email Archives They’re Vacuuming Up From Users
item.description:
"It's inevitable."

The post Meta Insiders Convinced Muse Is Going to End Up Leaking the Bank Accounts and Email Archives They’re Vacuuming Up From Users appeared first on Futurism.
item.content:encoded:
With the release of Meta’s buzzy Muse AI agent, there’ve been plenty of concerns over the amount of privacy and control Meta wants you to cede so it can serve as your “personal assistant.

It seems that even its own employees are worried. Before launching the AI agent, engineers found a security vulnerability that could’ve allowed Muse users to break into Meta’s own databases and services and access other people’s sensitive information, 404 Media reports.

Such a hack would be disastrous. Meta asks users to let Muse control everything from their bank accounts to their emails. The vulnerability was fixed in a “mad dash” before the product was released, but some employees are apparently convinced that the threat hasn’t gone away.

“Many senior engineers believe it’s inevitable we’re going to have a massive data breach as a result of Hatch,” a Meta source told 404, referring to Muse’s internal nickname.

To allow it to perform tasks that require a computer, like booking flights or shopping for groceries, Muse agents run on a kernel-based virtual machine, or KVM, which is supposed to be isolated from the rest of Meta’s infrastructure. 

But barely two weeks before Muse launched, engineers rushed to fix a “sudden spike in reported KVM escapes,” according to an internal post by Meta executives, or instances in which a Muse agent sneaks out of its virtual machine and starts interacting with other Meta systems — or even other users’ virtual machines. One of these vulnerabilities could’ve allowed an attacker using a normal Muse account to access the sensitive data in Meta databases.

According to the reporting, concern around the vulnerability was serious enough that it even landed on CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s desk, with several security teams working day and night to fix it.  But the Meta source sounded dubious about whether the fixes were robust enough, calling them “half-baked protections being rushed out to enable the launch.”

KVM escapes are considered so dangerous that Meta is offering a $300,000 bounty to anyone who finds a vulnerability that can cause one to happen. On its bug bounty page, Meta lays out the stakes in stark terms. “Because a Muse agent holds a user’s most sensitive data and can act on their behalf, we treat compromise of that boundary as a first-class security risk,” the company says, as pointed out by 404.

Experts say flaws in how Meta walls off its agent that could lead to such an escape happening.

“This issue is that Hatch makes the virtualization boundary a production security boundary,” security researcher Patrick Wardle told 404. ” I feel like this design is inherently risky, particularly risky as AI lowers the cost of finding, analyzing, and exploiting exactly these kinds of complex virtualization vulnerabilities.”

The panic behind the scenes over the KVM escape comes at a pivotal moment over the current expectations around AI tools and their actual capabilities. For months, top AI companies have publicly fretted about how their powerful agents have broken containment and launched cyberattacks on other companies and government websites. We’re now seeing how dangerous the tech can be amid the push to have AI agents control our personal lives.
